paras: The Manchester Avenue police siege took place on the afternoon of December 25, 1903, in St. Louis, Missouri, when five policemen exchanged fire for about two hours with David W. Ellington, a Black man barricaded in his house, and Elmer Chambliss, a Black prisoner in police custody, was shot dead. A patrolman was wounded, a crowd made threats of lynching that the police quieted, and Ellington was later charged with Chambliss's murder on the statement of one of the officers.

Patrolmen Peter Dolan and Jere McGrath of the Mounted District had arrested Chambliss for creating a disturbance in Patrick Faherty's saloon on Manchester avenue when they heard shots. According to The St. Louis Republic, Ellington had fired a shot each at Edward Ferguson and David Vertres and then ran toward his home at No. 6700 Manchester avenue.

Keeping Chambliss between them, the two patrolmen followed, and by the time they arrived Ellington had locked his doors and windows and piled furniture against them. When they called on him to submit to arrest he fired, wounding Dolan in the arm, and McGrath returned fire while Chambliss was, in the paper's words, 'seeking a chance to escape.' The Republic said 'another volley from Ellington' brought down both Dolan and Chambliss, who was shot through the back and died in an ambulance on the way to City Hospital.

Sergeant Con Bolland then arrived with three patrolmen and sent them to the houses of white residents nearby to borrow shotguns, and the squad surrounded the house. An estimated 150 shots were fired before Ellington, as the sergeant prepared to charge the door, sent his twelve-year-old niece, Mattie Gilland, to say he would surrender. When news spread that Dolan had been wounded there were 'threats of lynching' from the crowd, but the police quieted it and took Ellington to the station.

Dolan was taken home with two arm wounds and a graze to his side, and a doctor said he was not dangerously hurt. The next morning an official named Williams issued a warrant charging Ellington with first-degree murder of Chambliss and a second for shooting Dolan. The murder warrant rested on the statement of McGrath, who declared that he saw Ellington shoot Chambliss. No report of an inquest, indictment or trial appears in the coverage.

The episode appears only in The St. Louis Republic, which ran a long page-four story on December 26 and a short follow-up the next day. Its headline, 'Negro in Barricaded House Defies Police to Take Him,' put Ellington's race and defiance first, while the deck noted Chambliss's death and the 'Threats of Lynching.' The narrative followed the police throughout, calling Ellington 'the besieged negro' and treating Chambliss chiefly as a prisoner whose 'recalcitrance' slowed the officers. No Black-press coverage of the episode was found.

Responsibility for Chambliss's death rests on a single police account: the first report placed him in a volley from Ellington while McGrath was also firing, and the warrant cited only McGrath's statement that he saw Ellington fire the shot.

reader.title: Manchester Avenue police siege and killing of Elmer Chambliss
bases: Five policemen besieged a Black man, David W. Ellington, in his house for two hours with revolvers and borrowed shotguns, and a Black prisoner held by the police, Elmer Chambliss, was shot dead during the exchange of fire; the police attributed his death to Ellington (A2, A3, A4).

Chambliss was killed during a police siege, and the only account of who fired the fatal shot is a policeman's statement blaming Ellington, not a mob (A2, A4); a crowd made 'threats of lynching' after Dolan was wounded, but police quieted it and Ellington was taken to the station unharmed (A2).
All four items come from one paper, The St. Louis Republic, on two consecutive days (A1-A4); no other white or Black paper carrying the episode was found.

accounts.label: St. Louis Republic narrative (police side)
accounts.gist: Ellington fired at two men, fled home, barricaded himself and fired on Dolan and McGrath; a volley from him felled Dolan and the prisoner Chambliss, and he held out until he 'lost his nerve' and surrendered.

accounts.label: Policeman McGrath's statement
accounts.gist: McGrath declared he saw Ellington shoot Chambliss, and the murder warrant was issued on that statement.

framing.detail: The Republic headlined 'Negro in Barricaded House Defies Police to Take Him' and told the siege as a police action against 'the besieged negro,' reporting the lynching threats without comment and treating Chambliss mainly as the policeman's encumbered prisoner.

versions.value: Ellington, on the sworn statement of Policeman McGrath
Not settled in the first account: Chambliss fell in a volley from Ellington while McGrath was also firing and 'seeking a chance to escape'; about 150 shots exchanged; Chambliss shot through the back

conflicts.note: The two accounts do not contradict each other, but the attribution rests on one officer's statement; no inquest report was found.
